clue.text: An earful, as Hitler was in need of if the song is true?

parts.note: surface reading: a long harangue someone has to listen to

parts.words: as Hitler was in need of if the song is true?
parts.note: setter's reading: the wartime song says Hitler had only one testicle, so what he needed was a second one, a word in British slang that the answer starts with

explanation.surface: A wry question about whether the old wartime marching song about Hitler's anatomy was accurate.
explanation.walkthrough: The British wartime song 'Hitler Has Only Got One Ball' leaves him short of a testicle, and 'bollock' is British slang for one; the answer is a pun on that word, not a strict parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A severe telling-off is British slang for a scolding, which the recipient experiences as an earful.

clue.text: Churchman murdered by model — did Blair really think she was up to the job?

definitions.text: did Blair really think she was up to the job?

parts.note: Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, was murdered in his cathedral in 1170
the Model T Ford

explanation.surface: A churchman killed by a fashion model, followed by a jibe at a woman Blair appointed.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Beckett was Blair's surprise choice as Foreign Secretary in 2006.
explanation.definitionFit: The question describes Blair's Foreign Secretary, whose appointment was widely doubted, so it points to her by name.

clue.text: Old politician snapped "Tell an obnoxious person like Robert Maxwell"

parts.note: a Liberal, of the party that became the Liberal Democrats

indicators.note: something snapped is broken, so the letters of the quoted words are broken up and reset

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A veteran politician angrily tells someone to warn off a bully like the press baron Robert Maxwell.
explanation.walkthrough: The media tycoon Robert Maxwell was notorious for suing critics, Private Eye among them, for libel.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who brings a libel action is so called, and Maxwell, a serial litigant, was the obvious example for this magazine.

clue.text: Applying ring to member is visually stimulating work

parts.note: a ring is O-shaped
a member is a part of a body or whole

explanation.surface: A smutty hint at a ring on a man's member as a visual turn-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Applying ... to' only puts the ring before the member.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1960s style of abstract painting uses optical illusions to excite the eye, so it is literally visually stimulating.

clue.text: (& 18dn.) Unconsidered response, typical of tabloid press, a blow to the balls for someone?

definitions.text: Unconsidered response, typical of tabloid press
a blow to the balls for someone?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: jerking your knee up into a man's groin is a ... someone might give

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second, literal reading of the familiar phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names an automatic, thoughtless response, like the reflex kick when a doctor taps your knee.

clue.text: Caught sticking bar up Roger

indicators.note: in a down entry 'up' means read from the bottom, so the word is turned round

parts.note: to bar is to ban
to roger someone is British slang for having sex with them, i.e. to bed them

explanation.surface: Someone was caught in the act, sticking a bar somewhere uncomfortable belonging to a man named Roger.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger looks like a man's name, but it is the British slang verb for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: To be nabbed is informal for being arrested or seized, which is the same as being caught.

clue.text: Say "publicity" and bugger me the old English way

definitions.text: bugger me the old English way

parts.note: e.g., for example, is what you write in place of 'say'
an ad is a piece of publicity

explanation.surface: Someone who wants to sound quaint swears mildly while mentioning publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' with quotation marks looks like an instruction to speak aloud, but it is the abbreviation for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic oath is an old-fashioned exclamation of surprise, the period equivalent of the modern vulgar 'bugger me'.

clue.text: Labour forced here to fall behind after Gordon just started getting upper class

indicators.note: something that has just started has only its opening letter so far

parts.note: first letter only
U is the standard label for upper-class usage
to lag is to fall behind

explanation.surface: Labour under the newly installed Gordon Brown is forced to trail behind and grow posh.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Brown had just succeeded Blair as Labour leader; 'Labour' looks like the party but means hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet prison camps were places where inmates were made to do hard, forced labour.

clue.text: House of Windsor? Extremely dodgy and obnoxious!

indicators.note: 'extremely' points to the extremes of the word, its first and last letters

parts.note: outside letters only
nasty means obnoxious

explanation.surface: An anti-royalist outburst calling the royal family crooked and unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the British royal house as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A royal house is a ruling family line, and the Windsors are one such line of monarchs.

clue.text: Dull, stupid type of taxi banter at first? Decline!

parts.note: a cab is a taxi

indicators.note: 'at first' asks for only the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: first letter only
to age is to decline with the years

explanation.surface: A complaint about a boring cabbie's chatter, ending with an order to turn the conversation down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type of taxi' reads as one phrase, but 'type' belongs to the definition and 'of' merely joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a person who is dull and inert, like a vegetable, is called by this vegetable's name.

clue.text: Decadent place, honey capital — academic leaves

parts.note: an endearment: honey, baby

indicators.note: when someone leaves, they go out of the word, so those letters are removed

parts.note: the UK capital
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A sketch of a corrupt honey-trap city, from which a scholar sensibly departs.
explanation.walkthrough: The don comes out of the capital, leaving only its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient city became a byword for luxury and vice, so any place of decadence is called by its name.

clue.text: Windy type of bishop meeting drunken lecher

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: a drunken person staggers about, so the letters next to it lurch out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A long-winded cleric runs into a drunk womaniser.
explanation.definitionFit: A person troubled by wind who keeps bringing it up through the mouth is called this.

clue.text: Tetchy Archer starts to do what Archer does, tipping back port

indicators.note: tipping something back turns it over, so the assembled string is read from its end
'starts' means only the opening letters of the two words before it are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of both words
Jeffrey Archer, the novelist and Tory peer, was jailed for perjury, i.e. lying

explanation.surface: A grumpy Jeffrey Archer starting on his favourite activity while knocking back a glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Archer's 2001 perjury conviction is a Private Eye staple. 'Port' looks like the drink he tips back, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Israeli town on the Gulf of Aqaba is the country's only Red Sea harbour, a seaport.

clue.text: Nobody special, Stalin familiarly rants on the web about US money

parts.note: Stalin was nicknamed Uncle Joe

indicators.note: 'about' places one word around another, wrapping it

parts.note: online opinion pieces
a G, or grand, is American slang for a thousand dollars

explanation.surface: An ordinary internet ranter fulminates about American cash, as if he were a little Stalin.
explanation.walkthrough: G for a grand is US slang. The money sits inside the online rants, just before their last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the British stock name for a hypothetical average person, like America's John Doe.

clue.text: Nameless wanker Tom tossed, pulling together

indicators.note: things tossed in the air land in a jumble, so the letters are rearranged
without a name: N is the standard abbreviation for name, so that letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crude, schoolboy picture of an anonymous lout called Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: With its N dropped, the insult leaves five letters, which join Tom's three in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulling together is the idiom for cooperating, which is exactly what joint effort by a group means.

clue.text: PM, having a disastrous poll — held in awe somehow!

indicators.note: one thing held in another sits inside it
a disastrous result is a wreck, so the word after it is wrecked and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: 'somehow' means in some way not specified, so the word before it can be arranged any way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A prime minister suffers a dreadful election result yet is somehow still revered.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled poll goes inside the jumbled awe, between its second and third letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Robert Walpole is regarded as Britain's first Prime Minister, serving from 1721 to 1742.

clue.text: Duplicitous, his dodgy folio precedes gutless Blair

indicators.note: something dodgy is unsound or crooked, so these letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written
F is the abbreviation for folio

indicators.note: with the guts removed only the outside of the name survives, its first and last letters

parts.note: Blair's first name is Tony; only its outside letters stay

explanation.surface: A dig at Tony Blair's 'dodgy dossier' on Iraq, a document that came before the war.
explanation.walkthrough: The 2003 'dodgy dossier' made Blair's government a byword for spin. 'Blair' stands for his first name before the inside is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shifty looks evasive and untrustworthy, the manner of a person who is two-faced.

clue.text: One who's into sex objectively?

parts.note: surface reading: someone who takes a cool, detached view of sex
setter's reading: someone whose sexual interest centres on objects

explanation.walkthrough: 'Objectively' normally means impartially; read literally it means by way of objects.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person is aroused by inanimate things such as shoes or rubber, so their sex life revolves around objects.

clue.text: see 4dn.
Spunk container

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for nerve or courage
second meaning: a vessel for liquid

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the two words suggest something cruder; apart, each is a meaning of one word. In British slang to 'lose your bottle' is to lose your nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both British slang for courage and the everyday glass or plastic vessel for drinks.

clue.text: Nappy contents not hot — watch out for mites

indicators.note: 'not' says the following item is absent from the phrase

parts.note: what fills a used nappy (British for diaper)
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A warning about soiled nappies, now cold, and a reminder to watch out for bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch out for mites' sounds like a warning about insects, but mites are little children to be looked after.
explanation.definitionFit: To look after small children while their parents are out is to keep watch over the little ones.

clue.text: Wobbling tits, rude? Rubbish!

indicators.note: anything wobbling is unsteady and moving about, so the letters shift into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prudish reader is asked whether jiggling breasts are rude, and snorts that the idea is nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Debris and leftover waste matter are what this word names, so it is a synonym of rubbish.

clue.text: Teaser showing top of sizeable chest

indicators.note: in a down entry the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter only
a coffer is a strongbox or chest

explanation.surface: A flirtatious woman revealing the upper part of an ample bosom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teaser' and 'chest' paint a striptease, but the chest is a box for valuables and the teaser a mocker.
explanation.definitionFit: One who teases mocks or makes fun of people, which is what one who jeers does.

clue.text: Do something with your gifts — shut your face!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: put paper round presents
second meaning: British slang for 'be quiet!'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gifts' suggests talents, as in making use of them, but they are parcels.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both to enclose presents in paper and, as a rude British command, to stop talking.

clue.text: See those who swing both ways dance — endlessly amusing

indicators.note: with no end, the final letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: bisexuals, called bis for short
a hop is an informal dance
a rich joke is a very amusing one

explanation.surface: An invitation to watch a bisexual dance that is endlessly entertaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like the verb inviting you to watch, but it is the noun for a bishop's area of authority.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is the diocese or office governed by a bishop, the same thing as this word.

clue.text: S-stupid prat, our Dave

parts.note: the stammered opening letter, taken as written

indicators.note: something stupid is muddled and confused, so the word after it is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone stammers an insult at a fool, then claims him as one of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: Dave Spart is Private Eye's long-running parody of a ranting far-left activist, hence 'our'.
explanation.definitionFit: The magazine's own spoof columnist is named Dave, so 'our Dave' names the house character.

clue.text: Votes Conservative, hiding provisional concern

indicators.note: a phrase hiding something keeps it tucked inside, across the boundary between its words

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: An election report: people vote Tory while keeping some worry about a stopgap arrangement quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesco is Britain's biggest supermarket chain. 'Provisional' looks like 'temporary', but here it means dealing in provisions.
explanation.definitionFit: A concern is a business, and a grocer selling food supplies is a business in provisions.

clue.text: Also, getting penetrated by sailor is prohibited

indicators.note: being penetrated means having something pushed inside, so one word goes into the other

parts.note: too means also
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A smutty aside about a sailor's sexual conduct being against the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taboo is forbidden by custom, so it is banned or not allowed.

clue.text: Dubya's half having a puke — botched reshuffle

indicators.note: only half of the surname is wanted, so the other two letters are dropped

parts.note: Dubya is the nickname of US President George W Bush
taken as written

indicators.note: a botched job is messed up, so the word next to it is scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: George W Bush throwing up over a cabinet reshuffle that has gone wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half of the surname is kept. Bush's 2006 cabinet changes were described in the press as a botched shake-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A reorganisation of jobs, especially in a cabinet, is called a reshuffle or this hyphenated noun.

clue.text: Shortly down to one's Y-fronts almost?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is left off

parts.note: stripped to your underpants is to be wearing only your briefs; Y-fronts are a style of men's briefs

explanation.surface: Someone is almost undressed, stripped down to their underwear in no time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' looks like 'soon', but it is meant as 'briefly', 'in few words'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean in a few words, concisely, as when summarising something.

clue.text: As featured in the Sun, in fact, IT survey

indicators.note: 'in' says the wanted letters are contained within the words after it

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A tabloid story about a computing survey, as reported in a British newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid long famous for its topless Page 3 models.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sun's Page 3 pictures of bare breasts made them the paper's most notorious feature.

clue.text: Blair aide after outing, "Cut his balls off!"?

parts.note: a spin is a short trip out, as in a car
to doctor an animal is to castrate it

explanation.surface: A Downing Street adviser, after being publicly exposed, faces a furious demand for his castration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outing' suggests exposing someone, but it is a pleasure trip. Blair's press chief Alastair Campbell was the archetypal political spin merchant.
explanation.definitionFit: Blair's media advisers, who shaped how news about him was presented, were called by this name.
